title: Advanced network diagnostics with Wireshark
summary: Capture and read packets to prove where a network problem actually lives — client, network, or server. Use Wireshark display filters and the TCP analysis flags to separate loss, latency, and application stalls.
objectives: Capture traffic at the right point and with the right scope using netsh trace and Wireshark
Write precise display filters to isolate a single conversation
Read the TCP three-way handshake and identify where a connection fails
Use TCP analysis flags to distinguish packet loss from latency from app stalls
Measure round-trip time and time-to-first-byte from a capture
Decide from evidence whether the fault is client, network path, or server

quiz.q: A user reports a slow web app. The capture shows the SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK complete in 2 ms, but the server's first data packet arrives 4 seconds after the client's request. Where is the problem?
options: Packet loss on the network path
Server-side processing — the network and handshake are fine; it's time-to-first-byte
A duplex mismatch on the switch
quiz.why: A fast handshake rules out the connection path, and the 4-second gap before the first response byte is server think-time (time-to-first-byte). The network delivered the request promptly; the server was slow to answer.

quiz.q: Which Wireshark display filter isolates only the retransmissions and other TCP problem indicators?
quiz.why: tcp.analysis.flags surfaces Wireshark's expert TCP findings — retransmissions, dup ACKs, zero windows, out-of-order — letting you see loss and flow-control problems without reading every packet.

quiz.q: You see many 'TCP Dup ACK' followed by 'TCP Retransmission' for the same segment. What does this indicate?
options: The server is rejecting the connection
Packet loss on the path — the receiver keeps asking for a missing segment until it is resent
quiz.why: Duplicate ACKs are the receiver signalling a gap; the matching retransmission is the sender resending the lost segment. Repeated cycles are classic packet loss, pointing at the network path.

quiz.q: Why capture with 'netsh trace' or a tap rather than only on the affected client?
options: Capturing at two points lets you compare what was sent versus received and localise loss to a segment of the path
quiz.why: A single endpoint capture cannot tell you whether a missing packet was never sent or lost in transit. Capturing at both ends (or a tap) lets you compare and localise the loss to a specific path segment.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does a 'TCP Zero Window' message mean and whose problem is it?
quiz.answer: A Zero Window means the receiver has advertised a window of zero, telling the sender to stop because the receiver's buffer is full — so it is the receiving application's problem: it is not reading data off the socket fast enough.
quiz.why: Zero Window is flow control, not loss; it points at a slow-consuming application on the receiving side, not the network.

quiz.q: How would you prove from a capture that a 'network is slow' complaint is actually a DNS problem?
quiz.answer: Filter for dns and measure the time between each query and its response; if name resolution takes seconds (or queries retry against a failing server) while the subsequent TCP connection to the resolved IP is fast, the latency lives in DNS, not in the data path.
quiz.why: Isolating the DNS query/response timing separates name-resolution delay from connection and transfer delay, attributing the latency to the correct layer.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — Capture network traffic with netsh trace

body_markdown:
## Packets do not lie

When a network complaint reaches Tier 3, the argument is usually "it's the network" versus "it's the app." A **packet capture** settles it with evidence. The skill is not capturing — it is reading: knowing which handful of packets answer the question, and filtering out the thousands that do not.

## Capture at the right point and scope

Where you capture decides what you can conclude. A capture on only the affected client cannot distinguish *never sent* from *lost in transit*. Capture at both ends (or use a tap/SPAN port) so you can compare. On Windows you can capture without installing anything using **netsh trace**, then convert the `.etl` for Wireshark, or capture directly in Wireshark.

```powershell
# Lightweight built-in capture; reproduce the issue, then stop
netsh trace start capture=yes tracefile=C:\evidence\net.etl maxsize=512
# ... reproduce the problem ...
netsh trace stop
```

Keep captures short and scoped — a 30-second capture of one reproduction beats an hour of noise.

## Filter down to one conversation

Wireshark's power is its **display filters**. Start broad, then narrow to the single conversation that matters.

```text
ip.addr == 10.20.5.10 && tcp.port == 443
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0      # just the SYNs (connection starts)
dns                                            # name resolution timing
tcp.analysis.flags                             # all the TCP problem indicators
```

Right-click a packet and choose **Follow > TCP Stream** to see one conversation end to end.

## Read the handshake, then the timing

Every TCP connection opens with a three-way handshake: **SYN**, **SYN-ACK**, **ACK**. If the SYN goes unanswered, the connection never forms — a firewall or a dead server. If the handshake completes fast but the first data byte is slow, the network is fine and the **server think-time** (time-to-first-byte) is the problem. This single distinction resolves most "slow app" tickets.

## TCP analysis flags: loss vs latency vs stall

Wireshark's expert analysis labels the symptoms for you:

```text
TCP Retransmission / Fast Retransmission  -> packet loss on the path
TCP Dup ACK (repeated)                    -> receiver signalling a gap (loss)
TCP Zero Window                           -> receiver's buffer full (slow app)
TCP Out-Of-Order                          -> path reordering / multipath
```

Loss (retransmissions and dup ACKs) points at the **network path**. A **Zero Window** is flow control — the *receiving application* is not reading fast enough, so it is an app problem, not a network one. Latency with no loss and a clean window points at distance or a slow hop. **Out-of-order** segments suggest path reordering or load-balanced multipath, which can also trigger spurious retransmissions. Each pattern routes the ticket to a different owner, so name the pattern before you name a team.

## Your task

Reproduce a real or simulated slow/failing network operation. Capture it with `netsh trace` (or directly in Wireshark) for under a minute. In Wireshark, filter to the single conversation with an `ip.addr`/`tcp.port` filter, then Follow the TCP Stream. Measure: handshake time, time-to-first-byte, and any `tcp.analysis.flags` hits. Decide and write down whether the evidence shows packet loss (network path), a Zero Window (receiving app), DNS delay, or server think-time — and state which team you would route it to and why.

slides.title: Read the handshake first
bullets: Every connection opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
Unanswered SYN: firewall or dead server.
Fast handshake, slow first byte: server think-time.
This one distinction resolves most 'slow app' tickets.
slides.narration: Every T C P connection opens with a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. If the SYN goes unanswered, the connection never forms — that's a firewall or a dead server. But if the handshake completes in a couple of milliseconds and then the first data byte takes four seconds, the network is fine and the server's think-time is the problem. That single distinction — handshake versus time-to-first-byte — resolves most slow-app tickets on its own.

slides.title: Loss vs latency vs stall
bullets: Retransmissions and Dup ACKs: packet loss on the path.
Zero Window: receiver's buffer full — a slow app.
Latency with no loss: distance or a slow hop.
Each pattern routes to a different owner.
slides.code:
TCP Retransmission   -> packet loss
TCP Dup ACK          -> receiver signalling a gap
TCP Zero Window      -> receiving app too slow
TCP Out-Of-Order     -> path reordering
slides.narration: Wireshark's expert analysis labels the symptoms for you. Retransmissions and repeated duplicate ACKs mean packet loss on the network path. A Zero Window means the receiver's buffer is full — the receiving application isn't reading fast enough, so that's an app problem, not a network one. Latency with no loss and a healthy window means distance or a slow hop. Each of these patterns routes the ticket to a completely different owner, which is exactly what your RCA needs.

slides.title: Measure, don't eyeball
bullets: Use the Time column and delta times.
Measure handshake duration explicitly.
Measure time-to-first-byte after the request.
For DNS, time each query to its response.
slides.narration: Don't eyeball timing — measure it. Use Wireshark's time column and set it to show delta times between packets. Measure the handshake duration explicitly. Measure the gap between the client's request and the server's first response byte — that's your time-to-first-byte. And for a suspected name-resolution problem, measure the time between each d n s query and its answer. If resolution takes seconds while the data path is fast, you've just proven the latency lives in D N S.

slides.title: Client, path, or server?
bullets: Loss patterns: the network path owns it.
Zero Window: the receiving application owns it.
Slow first byte: the server owns it.
DNS delay: the resolver or DNS infra owns it.
slides.narration: Bring it together into an attribution. Loss patterns — retransmissions and dup ACKs — mean the network path owns the problem. A Zero Window means the receiving application owns it. A slow first byte after a clean handshake means the server owns it. And slow d n s responses mean the resolver or D N S infrastructure owns it. Your job is to read the capture, pick the pattern, and hand the ticket to the right team with the packets that prove it.
